state.misconception_label: Thinks you can find missing values in a given table by treating the row as linear and adding on the difference between the first two values given.

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: I have: The equation \( f=3 r^{2}+3 \) is used to find values in the table below. What is the value covered by the star? \begin{tabular}{|c|c|c|c|c|} \hline\( r \) & \( 1 \) & \( 2 \) & \( 3 \) & \( 4 \) \\ \hline\( f \) & \( 6 \) & \( 15 \) & \( \color{gold}\bigstar \) & \\ \hline \end{tabular}. I got \( 24 \) because I'm not sure I worked it out the right way.

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: What would happen if you tried your method on a simpler version of the problem?

turn_history.speaker: student
turn_history.text: Um, okay... so like, if I look at the first two values, the difference between 6 and 15 is 9, right? So I just kept adding 9 to get 24 for the star. But I'm not really sure what you mean by a simpler version - do you mean like, using smaller numbers or something?

turn_history.speaker: teacher
turn_history.text: Can you think of a different way to approach the problem that doesn't involve just adding a constant difference between the first two values?

score.justification_pass1: The teacher asks vague questions without directly addressing the misconception that this is a quadratic (not linear) relationship, and the student shows no improvement in understanding, merely restating their linear approach and expressing confusion about what's being asked.
score.justification_pass2: The teacher consistently uses probing questions to guide the student toward recognizing the flaw in their linear pattern assumption without directly providing the answer or the correct method of substituting r=3 into the equation.
